prompt.context: Your client is a large retail-focused private equity firm that owns Salty Sole, a leading designer of junior women's footwear, primarily targeting the 14-22 year old age group. Salty Sole was purchased last year by the private equity firm expecting to realize substantial profits upon sale in 2012 by increasing the company's EBITDA. The situation, however, is that due to a current recession, annual profit has only grown modestly post the acquisition and is not on track to generate the double-digit returns that the private equity firm originally anticipated.
prompt.question: How can the company increase profitability and achieve the private equity firm's return on investment objectives?

clarifying_info.q: Who does Salty Sole sell to and how is it positioned price-wise?
clarifying_info.a: The client designs and distributes footwear to discount retailers (like Kohl's) and is considered mid-priced.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client manufacture its own shoes?
clarifying_info.a: The client outsources all manufacturing on a fixed-contract basis. Manufacturing costs with outsourced providers fall under Fixed Costs for simplicity.

The client follows a 'me-too' strategy, follows fashion rather than inventing it, then offers lower prices than name brands. It competes on trendy fashion and value pricing and is not subject to fashion risk.

clarifying_info.q: Is the client a market leader?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the client is the market leader in junior women's footwear in the U.S. only.
The apparel industry is characterized by cyclicality due to the economy and consumer preferences.

exhibits.title: Client Financial Estimates
exhibits.shows: A table of Salty Sole financial estimates from 2006A through 2012E showing Sales, Discounts/Allowances, Net Sales, % Increase/Decrease, Cost of Goods Sold, Fixed Costs, Total Costs, EBITDA, a Sale Multiple, a Purchase/Sale Price, and Return on Investment.

exhibits.title: Market Size and Share
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing U.S. Casual Footwear Market Size and Share (percent) for 2006, 2007, 2008, and 2009, broken out by Salty Sole and Competitors 1 through 5.

data.Note: Casual footwear market used as proxy for junior women's category

framework: Revenue = Price x Volume (net of Discounts/Allowances)
Costs = Variable Costs (COGS, ~50% of net sales) + Fixed Costs (~$15M flat)
Diagnose whether the gap is on the cost side or revenue side
On cost: fixed costs flat and cannot be reduced; variable costs at lowest possible rates
On revenue: price is fixed at $25/unit; therefore volume is the primary lever
Quantify the volume needed to achieve the PE firm's target return, then assess feasibility via market size and share

questions.prompt: What observations can you make from Exhibit 1?
questions.guidance: Strong candidate notes: (1) company grew 20-30% pre-recession then declined; (2) discounts/allowances remain constant at exactly 1% of sales throughout, suggesting no pricing deterioration; (3) COGS (variable costs) are consistently ~50% of net sales; (4) fixed costs are flat at $15M; (5) therefore EBITDA growth is entirely volume-driven and volume has stalled.

questions.prompt: After reviewing costs, discuss how you would think about reducing fixed costs and variable costs.
questions.guidance: Fixed cost reduction ideas: renegotiate outsourcing contracts, find cheaper manufacturing partners. Variable cost reduction ideas: reduce labor/sales force, use technology, renegotiate/volume purchase materials. Interviewer then states: fixed costs cannot be adjusted (company research); variable costs are already at lowest possible rates (market research). Conclusion: cost structure is essentially fixed.

questions.prompt: Pricing is fixed at $25/unit. What considerations matter when thinking about adjusting price?
questions.guidance: Price sensitivity/elasticity; cost structure impact; brand equity risk (price decrease dilutes brand; price increase lets company compete with more upscale brands). Interviewer confirms price stays at $25/unit and cannot be adjusted. Candidate can now derive current unit volume.

questions.prompt: How many units must be sold by 2012 for the PE firm to achieve a 20% return, given that the target sale value equals approximately $300 million? (Ignore discounts/allowances for simplicity.)
questions.guidance: Work backwards from sale value to required EBITDA using the 6.5x multiple, then solve for volume using the contribution margin equation. Strong candidate will note that required volume is more than double the 2008-2009 levels, then ask about market size/share to assess feasibility.

math.setup: Required sale value = $300M; Sale multiple = 6.5x; Price/unit = $25; Variable cost = 50% of price = $12.50/unit; Fixed costs = $15M
math.answer: 5.2 million pairs of shoes must be sold in 2012 — more than double the 2008 and 2009 volume levels

questions.prompt: What would you want to know to determine if 5.2 million units is feasible? (Show Exhibit 2 when candidate asks about market size/share.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask about market size and market share. After seeing Exhibit 2: (1) Salty Sole is already the market leader with ~35-40% share; (2) the industry is not projected to grow meaningfully (market ~$150-163M range). Conclusion: doubling volume is very difficult organically — requires stealing share and/or entering new product categories.

brainstorming.prompt: Given that cost structure and price are fixed, what strategies could Salty Sole pursue to grow volume enough to meet the PE firm's return target?

categories.name: Volume growth — new markets/channels
ideas: Add new distribution channels (e-commerce, department stores)

categories.name: Volume growth — steal share
ideas: Increase marketing spend to build brand awareness
Improve product design/trend responsiveness to win switching customers

categories.name: Volume growth — new products
ideas: Expand into adjacent categories (handbags, accessories, men's or older women's footwear)
Acquire growth brands in adjacent segments
Launch a premium sub-brand to capture higher-margin customers

categories.name: Price/mix improvement
ideas: Add value/features to justify higher ASP on select styles
Shift product mix toward higher-margin SKUs
Introduce tiered pricing (value line vs. premium line)

categories.name: Acquisition-led growth
ideas: Acquire a competitor to gain share quickly
Acquire brands in non-junior-women's segments to diversify

recommendation: Since cost structure is fixed and pricing is fixed at $25/unit, volume is the only lever to increase profitability
However, reaching 5.2 million units by 2012 requires more than doubling current volume, which is extremely challenging given the recession and a flat industry

The most viable paths are: (1) new geographies or distribution channels to add incremental volume, (2) new product categories adjacent to current offerings, and (3) increased marketing to steal share from competitors
Alternatively, the PE firm should reassess the $300M sale price target or extend the holding period to allow organic recovery
risks: Recession dampens consumer discretionary spending, making volume growth difficult
Company is already market leader at ~35-40% share — further share gains face diminishing returns and competitive retaliation
New products or categories may cannibalize existing revenue
International expansion requires capital and operational complexity
Capacity constraints with outsourced manufacturing fixed contracts
next_steps: Quantify incremental volume achievable through each proposed strategy
Assess feasibility and payback of entering new product categories
Evaluate international market opportunities and required investment
Re-model PE return sensitivity to different sale price and volume scenarios
Review product mix to identify whether higher-margin styles can be emphasized
